questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Cofactor in a NxN Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
First, to get the minor of ${d}_{34}$, we remove the $3$rd row and $4$th column: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 2 & ∗ & -1 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 & ∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗ & 6 & ∗ \\ 4 & 0 & 3 & ∗ & 3 \\ 11 & 3 & 0 & ∗ & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the minor is 

$$
{M}_{34}=|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 11 & 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|.
$$

Now, the cofactor of ${d}_{34}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{34} & =(-1)^{3+4}{M}_{34} \\  & =-{M}_{34} \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 11 & 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Cofactor in a NxN Matrix

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets
questions.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={1}$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${X}_{2}={1,2}$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${X}_{3}={1,2,3}$

and so on. 

Notice that ${X}_{i}$ contain all the integers between $1$ and $i.$ So, every natural number $i$ belong to the sets ${X}_{i},\,{X}_{i+1},\,{X}_{i+2},…$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=N.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination
questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=0 \\  & y+2z=0 \\  & x+y+3z=1\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Dot Product of Two Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the dot product, we add up the products of corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot s & ={r}_{1}\cdot {s}_{1}+{r}_{2}\cdot {s}_{2}+{r}_{3}\cdot {s}_{3}+{r}_{4}\cdot {s}_{4}+{r}_{5}\cdot {s}_{5} \\  & =1\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-4)+3\cdot 1+5\cdot 1+2\cdot (-2) \\  & =3+4+3+5-4 \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $F(-5,-2,4)$ and $G(3,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $F$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=f+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $f$ is the position vector of $F.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $F(-5,-2,4)$ and $G(3,-1,1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{FG} \\  & =⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨-5,-2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093211/assets/fc3c0c02be98834937150e6bee5a52ac14246bc128b189d3c095269f788d97a9.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+{x}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+6x)\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\frac{(\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}]-[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\frac{(-\pi /4)^{3}}{3}+6(-\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =(0+\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}+\frac{3\pi }{2})-(0-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{192}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{96}+3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine

questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- The matrix $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix. So, it is not invertible.

- For the matrix $B$, we have

$$
det(B)=4\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 3=2.
$$

Because $det(B)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $B$ is invertible.

- For the matrix $C$, we have

$$
det(C)=4\cdot 9-3\cdot 12=0.
$$

Because $det(C)=0,$ we conclude that $C$ is not invertible.

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ do not have an inverse.

questions.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+3\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (2x+3)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =(2x+3)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =-(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Tall Ellipse
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093211/assets/b12eb6672d263655f9f77eaafbf486a7be5bf9b7673c73fd0d75382d192a658b.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

{{field-1}}$=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and the vertical radius has length $b=\frac{9}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\frac{9}{2})}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\frac{9}{4})}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\frac{81}{4})} & =1 \\ \frac{4{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{81} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Determining the Equation of a Tall Ellipse
